chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who says, 'Upon me is a vow.' He said, 'It is not binding until he specifies the vow, saying: 'Upon me is a fast for Allah,' or 'I will give charity,' or 'I will free a slave,' or 'I will offer a sacrifice.' If the man says, 'I will offer this food,' this is not binding; rather, the sacrifice offered is the camel (or large livestock).'

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Jamil ibn Salih, who said: 'I had a female servant in Medina, and her menstruation began. I made a vow to Allah: 'If she menstruates, upon me is [a vow].' I learned that she had indeed menstruated before I made the vow. I wrote to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was in Medina, and he answered me: 'If she had menstruated before the vow, there is no obligation upon you; but if she had menstruated after the vow, then the obligation is upon you.'

key_terms.الْبُدْنُ: Camel or large livestock used for sacrifice
key_terms.نَذْرٌ: Vow (a pledge to perform a specific act of worship or charity for Allah's sake)

ai.seo_question: What makes a religious vow (nadh) binding according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic requirement of specificity (*takhassus*) for a vow to be binding, distinguishing between general declarations and those specifying acts like fasting, charity, or animal sacrifice. The second report illustrates the principle of temporal causality in vows, where the obligation attaches only if the condition occurs after the vow is made, reflecting the Shia emphasis on intent and precise wording. This aligns with the broader legal theory that vows are voluntary obligations (*ibadat*) requiring clear definition to avoid ambiguity (*gharar*).
